name: Omar Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree, and I maintain a live-event cue app for a tech company. I use AI every day for tests and have years of experience, though I am an ordinary developer who still checks changes against rehearsal sound. Rosa manages a restaurant; we have two school-age children, a mortgage and about three months saved, so a quiet restaurant week matters at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the live-event cue app still needs someone to hear whether the sound starts at the right moment. I use AI every day to draft tests, then listen to a rehearsal recording before I release a change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn ordinary mid-level developer pay and have about three months of basic expenses saved. My partner Rosa manages a restaurant with changing shifts, so the mortgage and two children keep me alert even when software barely changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing missed sound cues and ask the event crew for one rehearsal failure each week. We would leave 100 monthly in the emergency account if my pay and Rosa’s shifts hold, instead of buying another speaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about the restaurant side of our income, not this mild AI story. A quiet dining room can change our month faster than a new coding tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of cue goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At a school concert, the lights changed but the entrance music started ten seconds late. The children stood in silence while I traced which cue number the app had skipped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you own a speaker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to help with sound at small venues, and I still have a compact kit. I would not buy more gear until paid work justifies it.

say: I tell coworkers a **sound cue** must be checked by listening, not only reading code.
I test **AI-drafted checks** against rehearsal recordings.
think: I have **three months saved** on ordinary mid-level pay.
I worry Rosa’s **restaurant shifts** can move our mortgage budget quickly.
do: **Keep fixing** missed cues and review one crew complaint weekly.
**Save 100 monthly** if both incomes hold; delay buying another speaker.
feel: **Uneasy** about restaurant income despite mild AI change.
S0.quote: The children stood in silence while I traced which cue number the app had skipped.
fieldNote: His **event-sound background** gives him an ear for errors that code checks can miss.
Three months saved cushions **variable restaurant shifts**, but he still watches the mortgage.

steps.text: Keep fixing sound-cue bugs and review event crew complaints
Save 100 monthly if both incomes hold
Delay buying another speaker until paid work justifies it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that AI writing code and booking customers can cut into both our event platform and Rosa’s restaurant hours. I would ask the workplace group for a written staffing plan before managers say everyone will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The smaller cue fixes I do could go first, and Rosa’s bookings might be automated while her shift hours fall. A three-month cushion will not carry both our wages if they shrink together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI way to compare sound cues with rehearsal timing, using old recordings we have permission to use. I’d join the workplace group’s staffing meeting in the first year and ask who gets paid for late-night release checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about both incomes, even though I like the tool. I want technology to shorten a late shift, not turn two people’s hours into one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the new check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the school concert where the music was late and compare the AI timing mark with what the stage manager wrote. If it misses ten seconds, I will not call it accurate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rosa say about restaurant bookings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would say an automated booking can still leave a table empty when a group does not arrive. I would not write her a plan; she knows her floor better than I do.

say: I want a **written staffing plan** for event code and restaurant bookings.
I would ask our **workplace group** who is paid for late release checks.
think: I expect **small cue fixes** to be automated first.
I fear Rosa’s **booking hours** and my coding hours could shrink together.
do: **Learn AI cue timing** on permitted old rehearsal recordings this month.
**Join workplace group talks** about staffing and paid late-night release checks.
feel: **Anxious** about two incomes, despite liking the tool.
S1.quote: I want technology to shorten a late shift, not turn two people’s hours into one.
fieldNote: Daily AI use does not hide his **two-earner exposure** to code and booking automation.
The **permitted recordings** provide a concrete test of new cue-timing learning.

steps.text: Learn AI cue-timing checks on old rehearsal recordings with permission
Join workplace group talks about staffing and paid release checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write most of the event code I maintain, while robots that handle stage equipment arrive about 2031. Rosa’s booking and planning work could change in 2028 too, though serving guests remains hands-on for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer job might end, and the restaurant might cut Rosa’s planning hours as software takes them. Three months saved gives us little time to replace two parts of the household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our workplace group now to seek written notice and severance terms, and I’d stop shopping for a larger sound desk. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I’d apply for paid venue-sound shifts only if bookings exist and the net pay covers our mortgage share and bills; I’d claim any income support we qualify for while looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed, even with a bag of sound cables ready. A handful of gigs is not the same as a regular pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the children about the sound desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say we are keeping the gear we have and putting house bills first. A new desk is a want, not a reason to worry them about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could venue shifts last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe until more capable robots reach stage work around 2031, and I do not know how many shifts are available. I would not borrow for a big rig on that guess.

say: I tell coworkers **thinking AGI by 2028** reaches event code and restaurant planning.
I know **stage robots around 2031** follow the first software shock.
think: I expect my **developer job** and Rosa’s planning hours could both shrink.
I know **three months saved** cannot replace a regular pay slip for long.
do: **Seek written notice** and severance terms through our workplace group now.
**Keep current sound gear** and skip buying a larger desk.
**Apply for venue shifts** only if displaced after 2028, bookings exist and net pay covers bills; claim eligible income support.
feel: **Alarmed** by two income risks and uncertain gig bookings.
S2.quote: A handful of gigs is not the same as a regular pay slip.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 thinking work** from stage robots that come around 2031.
Venue gigs are a **conditional bridge**, requiring bookings and net income after costs.

steps.text: Ask the workplace group for written notice and severance terms
Keep the current sound gear instead of buying a larger desk
Apply for paid venue-sound shifts if displaced after 2028 and bookings yield bill-covering net pay
Claim income support only if eligible after a job loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 gives us time to see which live events still pay people to run sound. Robots may move stage equipment around 2034, so I would not call mixing a permanent refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can build a proper record of paid event work while I still draw a developer wage, but my code still faces 2031. Rosa and I could save more if both our earnings stay steady, though restaurant hours change with the season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask two venues this year whether they have paid weekend sound shifts, and accept at most one a month if booked and Rosa can cover childcare. I’d keep a ledger of net gig pay after travel and save 120 monthly from wages only if both incomes hold; after 2031 I’d seek paid venue operations only if my developer job ends and openings cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious but more deliberate. I want actual pay entries in the ledger before I call sound a second job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only one shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A Saturday away leaves Rosa with both children after a restaurant week. I would not make a second income by handing my partner Rosa a second unpaid shift at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the venues have no work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current job and let the ledger stay empty. I would not buy equipment or count money that has not arrived.

say: I want **paid venue work** tested before AGI reaches my code in 2031.
I know **stage robots around 2034** may later reduce physical setup work.
think: I could build **real gig records**, though my code faces AGI in 2031.
I might save **more cash** if both incomes continue despite changing shifts.
do: **Ask two venues** about paid weekend shifts and take one monthly only if booked and childcare is covered.
**Record net gig pay** and save 120 from wages only if both incomes hold.
**Seek paid venue operations** if displaced after 2031 and vacancies cover bills.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate** about testing real paid work.
S3.quote: I would not make a second income by handing my partner Rosa a second unpaid shift at home.
fieldNote: He limits weekend work to **one booked shift** and Rosa’s childcare capacity.
The **net-pay ledger** separates actual side income from hopeful numbers, including travel costs and the value of family time.

steps.text: Take at most one paid venue shift monthly if booked and childcare is covered
Save 120 monthly from wages only if both incomes hold
Seek paid venue-operations vacancies if displaced after 2031 and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 lets workers bargain for training and build more than one source of income. Robots for stage equipment may follow around 2039, but the code changes earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might pay down the mortgage and learn whether sound work suits our family, but AI can plan events and robots can later handle equipment. I will not put our children’s school costs on a promise that gigs last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining event code and take paid sound shifts only when booked and Rosa can cover the children. We would put 150 monthly toward the mortgage buffer if both incomes hold, separately from any net gig pay; if my developer role ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid venue-production roles only if vacancies remain and wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about the distant job change but less worried about next year’s pay. I want a record of real customers before I try to make sound work my main income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the sound record convincing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve paid events with repeat venue calls and net income after travel. A busy calendar with no money left at home is not a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask workers to bargain even if you have gigs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because my coworkers without a sound kit need paid time to learn too. I would bring the request to our workplace group while I still have a wage.

say: I want **paid learning time** negotiated before full AGI reaches event code in 2036.
I know **stage robots around 2039** follow the coding change.
think: I could lower the **mortgage balance** if both incomes hold.
I know **gigs may not last** once AI planning and stage robots spread.
do: **Maintain** code, take booked sound shifts with Rosa’s childcare, and request paid learning through our workplace group while employed.
**Save 150 monthly** toward the mortgage buffer if both incomes hold, apart from gig pay.
**Apply for paid production** only if displaced after 2036 and vacancies cover bills.
feel: **Uneasy later**, with next year’s income looking steadier.
S4.quote: A busy calendar with no money left at home is not a business.
fieldNote: He wants **twelve paid events** and net income before treating sound as primary work.
The **mortgage buffer** comes from continuing wages, independent of uncertain gig pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my code work and Rosa’s booking hours could change together. Written notice, eligible income support and real paid venue shifts that cover our bills would help while we search; I would not buy more sound gear on a guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what weekend work costs at home. If Rosa covers the children after a restaurant week, I owe that time back rather than count every gig as free money. Weekend sound work costs my partner Rosa childcare time after her restaurant week.

headlineQuote: Weekend sound work costs my partner Rosa childcare time after her restaurant week.
portrait: Omar is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, ordinary pay and three months of expenses saved.
He and Rosa cover **two children** and a mortgage while restaurant shifts make income uneven.
He uses **AI daily** on event cues and checks results by listening to recordings.
He tests **paid sound gigs** with booking, childcare and net-pay gates instead of buying more equipment.
The **2028 case** worries him most because both code and restaurant planning income may shrink.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce his developer wage and Rosa’s restaurant planning hours together.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, eligible income support and paid venue bookings with bill-covering net pay would help.
